hotel.explainer.title: What is the Hotel Lobby AI filter?
hotel.explainer.origin: The trend comes from a real performance. On June 17, 2022, the COLORS YouTube channel released Quavo and Takeoff performing their song "Hotel Lobby" against a flat orange backdrop, trading lines on a single microphone hung from the ceiling. In September 2026 creators on TikTok and X began using AI video tools to swap the two rappers for friends, couples, celebrities, fictional characters and even pets while keeping the original moves, lip-sync and audio — and the "Hotel Lobby AI" meme took off.
hotel.explainer.one: Two subjects stand on opposite sides of one hanging microphone while the camera holds steady. One leads, the other reacts, and then they trade the moment. Friends, partners or family members can appear together even when their source photos were taken separately.
hotel.explainer.two: This page makes that look for you. Choose two portraits, decide who appears on each side and optionally add a styling note. We compose the scene with GPT Image 2 and animate it with DreamActor motion transfer, which carries over the reference performance and its audio.
hotel.explainer.three: Think of it as a short scene. A good result keeps each person recognizable, gives both people room and places the microphone between them. Orange walls, warm light and a steady camera unify the setup. Results vary with the model and photos, so review the clip before posting.
hotel.guide.title: Make your Hotel Lobby AI duet look more like your people
hotel.guide.intro: A precise prompt helps, but the photos you choose set the ceiling for the final scene. These checks can reduce common identity and composition problems before you generate.
hotel.guide.photos.title: Start with useful portraits
hotel.guide.photos.text: Use sharp images with full faces and enough clothing to guide the scene. Avoid heavy filters, sunglasses, crowded backgrounds and cropped faces. Similar lighting and perspective can make the duet feel more consistent. If one portrait is a close-up and the other shows a full body, crop or replace one so the references match more closely. Neutral expressions leave more room for a believable reaction. Only transform images you have permission to use.
hotel.guide.motion.title: Keep the action readable
hotel.guide.motion.text: Describe one short exchange: a lead singer, a listening reaction and a handoff. Ask for natural mouth movement and small gestures while the camera stays centered. State whose lips move in each beat so the performers do not appear to sing the same line at once. Fast turns and sudden cuts can make faces or left-right positions harder to preserve.
hotel.guide.review.title: Inspect the first take
hotel.guide.review.text: Watch the clip before sharing. Confirm that A stays left, B stays right and the microphone stays between them. Check for warped hands, merged faces, extra people or changing outfits. Watch once with the sound off: the handoff should still make visual sense. If a face changes midway, shorten the scene before adding more movement. If the scene breaks, simplify your direction and try again.
hotel.prompt.title: Hotel Lobby AI Prompt (Copy and Paste)
hotel.prompt.one: For a Hotel Lobby AI duet, the starter prompt names the main visual anchors: a vertical 9:16 frame, a matte-orange booth, two separate people, one black microphone, soft light and a locked camera. It also asks the model to preserve faces and outfits and avoid side swaps, added people, captions and watermarks. These constraints give the generator a clearer shot list than a vague request to make two photos sing together.
hotel.prompt.two: Use the direction field for one styling detail, such as outfits, accessories or expressions. Keep it short so the core composition still leads — the booth, the center microphone and left-right placement are fixed by the base prompt. If the first result is off, change one thing at a time and generate again.
hotel.prompt.copy_text: Two people from my two reference photos perform a duet in a seamless burnt-orange recording booth. Person A (photo 1) stands on the left, Person B (photo 2) on the right, facing each other across one black microphone hanging at face level in the exact center. Vertical 9:16, static centered camera, soft even studio light, framed from the knees up. A sings the first line while B listens and nods; B takes the next line while A reacts; then they share the mic. Natural lip-sync and small hand gestures. Keep each face, hairstyle and outfit unchanged. No side swaps, no extra people, no captions, no watermark.
hotel.faq.title: Hotel Lobby AI FAQ
hotel.faq.one.question: Can I generate the duet video on this page?
hotel.faq.one.answer: Yes. Sign in, upload one photo for each side and press Generate. The scene is ready in under a minute and the finished video in about 3–5 minutes. Each video uses credits.
hotel.faq.two.question: What happens to my photos?
hotel.faq.two.answer: When you press Generate, your two photos are resized in your browser and sent to our AI provider (fal.ai) to create the scene and the video. They are not uploaded before you press Generate. Only use photos you have permission to use.
hotel.faq.three.question: Can I make the duet with two separate photos?
hotel.faq.three.answer: Yes. Use one clear reference for each person, with A on the left and B on the right. Identity preservation depends on the generator and photos, so inspect the result.
hotel.faq.four.question: Why do the faces or positions change in my result?
hotel.faq.four.answer: Models can drift when references are unclear or actions are busy. Use visible faces, remove camera moves and describe a shorter exchange. Repeat left-right placement and request one continuous shot. A usable clip may take several tries.
hotel.faq.five.question: Can I use photos of a couple or friends?
hotel.faq.five.answer: Yes. The orange booth can frame a couple, friends or family — including a parent and their child, as long as you're that child's parent or legal guardian. Change the performance direction but keep identities separate. Get permission from everyone pictured and identify the result as AI-generated when you share it.
hotel.faq.six.question: How much does a Hotel Lobby AI video cost?
hotel.faq.six.answer: Every generation uses credits, and the exact amount is shown on the button and in the pricing section. Choose a one-time pack or subscribe monthly. If a generation fails, the credits go back to your balance automatically.
hotel.faq.seven.question: What is the hotel lobby AI trend?
hotel.faq.seven.answer: It is a two-person duet scene in an orange recording booth. One person starts a line beside a hanging microphone, and the other responds. Creators often use two separate photos to plan a shared AI video scene.
hotel.faq.eight.question: Is the video generated on this site?
hotel.faq.eight.answer: Yes. The scene preview and the finished video are both generated here on Hotel Lobby AI — you don't need any other app or account. Finished videos are saved in My videos.

admin.funnel.footnote.title: Definitions
admin.funnel.footnote.unique: Every step counts unique visitors (hl_did cookie), not impressions; percentages under each step are relative to visitors in the same row. The daily table de-duplicates within each UTC+8 day.
admin.funnel.footnote.visit: Visitors = browsers that opened the generator page (/ or /ai-livestream, event hl_home_view, sent from the browser; bot user agents dropped).
admin.funnel.footnote.first_touch: Source / country = external referrer or utm_source and cf-ipcountry at the visitor's first event, pinned by cookie. Visitors who came before tracking shipped are attributed to their first visit after it.
admin.funnel.footnote.checkout: Sent to payment = the server created a payment session (/api/payment/checkout); provider is the one actually used.
admin.funnel.footnote.paid: Payers / revenue come from the order table (status = paid, by paid_at), so webhook-only payments count. Source/country use the payer's earliest event, build uses their latest checkout; payers with no events show as unknown. Revenue sums order amounts with no currency conversion.
admin.funnel.footnote.provider: Provider table is by order creation time: payment success = orders paid ÷ orders created (abandoned checkouts count as unpaid).
admin.funnel.footnote.build: Build = git commit of the page/server that sent the event.
admin.funnel.footnote.compare: Today vs yesterday compares the same clock time: today 00:00 → now against yesterday 00:00 → this time yesterday (UTC+8).
admin.funnel.footnote.excluded: Excluded: test user {ids} and every visitor id that user has used.
admin.funnel.section.history: Traffic since launch (Cloudflare Web Analytics + orders)
admin.funnel.history.synced: Traffic imported through {day}. Run `npx tsx scripts/sync-traffic.ts` to refresh.
admin.funnel.history.not_synced: No traffic imported yet. Run `npx tsx scripts/sync-traffic.ts`.
admin.funnel.footnote.history: Traffic since launch: browser page views and visits come from Cloudflare Web Analytics (a JS beacon only real browsers send, so crawlers are excluded) imported by scripts/sync-traffic.ts. It is sampled: page views are the steadier number; visits (page loads arriving from outside the site) are a rough estimate at this traffic level, so no conversion rate is computed from them. Free previews = distinct devices (the feature ran Oct 2–9). Sign-ups, started checkout (distinct users who created an order), payers and revenue come from the user and order tables. The CN/HK switch only removes those countries from page views and visits.
admin.funnel.footnote.history_referrer: Referrers come from the browser's Referer header. ChatGPT strips it, so most ChatGPT clicks show as direct here; the user table's utm_source (chatgpt.com) is the reliable ChatGPT signal. /admin pages are excluded from traffic and the top pages list.

gc.resources.guide.formulas.title: Make SUM and IF work for you.
gc.resources.guide.formulas.description: Use SUM for a total and IF to turn a number into a useful decision.
gc.resources.guide.formulas.step1: In a blank sheet, enter Amount in A1. Put 120, 85 and 45 in A2, A3 and A4.
gc.resources.guide.formulas.step2: Select A5 and enter =SUM(A2:A4). Press Enter. The result should be 250.
gc.resources.guide.formulas.step3: In B2, enter =IF(A2>100,"Review","OK"). A2 contains 120, so B2 should show Review.
gc.resources.guide.formulas.step4: Change A2 to 90. A5 should update to 220 and B2 to OK. Save an XLSX copy when you finish.

gc.resources.guide.analysis.step2: Select A1:B4 and use the chart command from the toolbar or Insert menu. Choose a column chart, then check that the amounts and category labels match the cells.
gc.resources.guide.analysis.step3: With the same source range, open the PivotTable command. Use Category as the row field and Amount as a value field, summarized by SUM.
gc.resources.guide.analysis.step4: Check the summary: Travel should total 165 and Supplies 85. Save the workbook and reopen a copy to verify the result.

gc.story.title: Your GridCraft ArtCraft guide.
gc.story.intro: GridCraft is the spreadsheet application from ArtCraft, an open-source software studio. Written in Rust, it combines an Excel-style ribbon, worksheet tabs and a formula bar with a calculation engine that runs on desktop computers and in the browser through WebAssembly.
gc.story.context: Think of it as another place to explore a workbook, rather than a promise that every Excel feature will behave identically. It is useful to try a household budget, a class gradebook or a sales summary and see how the workflow feels. This independent site brings together the official browser build, practical tutorials and direct release links. The software comes from ArtCraft; the guidance and website are maintained separately.
gc.story.open.title: Open an XLSX. Keep the original.
gc.story.open.text: Start with a copy of a small Excel workbook. In the GridCraft online editor, use the file-open control to select an XLSX file from your computer. Inspect the sheet names, column widths, number formats and a few formulas before making changes. XLSX is GridCraft’s native format, but an alpha application can interpret complex files differently. For everyday experiments, a short expense sheet is a better first test than a business-critical financial model. When you finish, use Save As to download an XLSX copy and reopen it to check your work.
gc.story.formulas.title: Let the cells do the calculation.
gc.story.formulas.text: Build confidence with a calculation you can verify yourself. Enter a few amounts, total them with SUM, then use IF to label a value above a chosen threshold. Change one source cell and watch the result update. The upstream project documents more than 500 worksheet functions, including dynamic array features, LET and LAMBDA. That breadth gives you room to explore, but it does not replace checking your own results. Workbooks using specialist Excel functions, external data or macros need separate evaluation. Our formula tutorial starts with small, reproducible examples.
gc.story.analysis.title: Find the story behind a table.
gc.story.analysis.text: A useful spreadsheet makes a pattern easier to see. Keep one kind of record per row, use clear column headings and give dates and amounts consistent formats. Then explore a chart for a quick comparison, or a PivotTable to group repeated categories. GridCraft’s sample sales workbook shows how tables and charts can share the same source data. For a budget, compare planned and actual spending; for a gradebook, inspect averages before assigning labels. Begin with a simple question, keep the underlying values visible and verify that a summary includes the intended rows.

GridCraft and Excel: Open, Edit and Save XLSX Files
Use Excel files in GridCraft with a practical XLSX workflow. Check formulas, charts, macros and format limits before saving a workbook back to Excel.
Excel compatibility
12 min read

GridCraft can open and save Excel .xlsx workbooks. The useful question is whether your particular workbook survives the trip: its formulas, formatting and charts need checking after a save and reopen. This guide gives you a repeatable way to make that check without replacing your original.
Start with a copy and a clear baseline

Choose a small workbook you understand: a spending sheet, an inventory list or a simple project tracker. Before opening it in another app, record the sheet names, one important total and one representative formula. A screenshot of a chart or formatted table also gives you something concrete to compare.

Keep the original file in a separate folder. Call your working copy something like budget-gridcraft-test.xlsx. This guide references the official v0.19.1 release. The bundled browser editor can have a different version; check its version label and match your test to the build you actually intend to use.
Find the desktop builds on the homepage
Open, edit and save an Excel workbook

Open the GridCraft editor and launch the workspace. Choose File → Open and select your test .xlsx file. The web build uses the browser’s file picker; opening a file does not create a shared cloud document.
Check the sheet tabs and your baseline total before editing. Select a formula cell and inspect its formula bar, rather than checking only the number displayed in the grid.
Make one controlled change, such as increasing a known expense by 10. Verify that the dependent total changes by the same amount. Start with a simple reference before testing a complex formula.
Choose File → Save As and save a new .xlsx copy. In the browser, this downloads a file. Check your downloads folder and the actual filename; a second save may produce a numbered copy.

Reopen the downloaded copy in Excel. Compare the changed total, the formula itself, the number formats and any charts you rely on. If Excel offers to repair the file, keep the original and investigate before using the exported copy.

Check more than the total

A workbook can calculate the right total while still losing an important presentation detail. Compare chart categories, axis labels, legend entries and the data range. For PivotTables, compare the source data, filters, subtotals and grand total. A working screenshot is a reference, not a guarantee that every imported Excel chart will look the same.

Also inspect dates, percentages, leading zeros in identifiers and hidden sheets. If the workbook depends on external connections, refresh behavior or a data model, test those requirements separately. Preserving a file part is different from executing the workflow behind it.
GridCraft chart selected with its data range highlighted and chart formatting controls visible
Compare both the plotted values and chart formatting after an XLSX round trip. Screenshot: ArtCraft.
Reconcile a real workbook in three passes

First, check structure. Count the worksheets and compare their names and order with the original. Look for hidden sheets, named ranges and the source range of any summary. A missing supporting sheet may not be obvious on the first tab. Make a short checklist of the parts the workbook needs to do its job, then inspect those parts before testing individual formulas.

Second, check meaning. Dates should still be dates, a product code such as 00127 should still identify the same product, and a percentage should keep the same scale. Compare a few ordinary rows and the edge cases: blanks, zero values, negative amounts and the last populated row. A total alone cannot tell you whether a code lost its leading zeros or whether one category moved into the wrong group.

Third, check behavior. Change a source input and see whether the relevant summary updates. Remove your test change, save and reopen, then repeat one calculation. Record the source application, source version, GridCraft version and filename with the result. That small record makes it possible to reproduce a difference instead of guessing which of several downloaded copies you checked.
A minimal test record. Replace these example quantities with numbers from your own workbook.
Diagnose a mismatch before changing more cells

If a formula produces an unexpected value, compare the formula text first. Check its range endpoints, sheet reference and whether a supposed number is stored as text. Then reduce the calculation to a smaller example with two or three inputs. If the smaller example works but the original does not, add the original dependencies back one at a time. This helps distinguish an input problem from a function or reference problem.

If the numbers agree but the appearance differs, inspect the underlying values separately from their display format. A stored value of 0.25 and a displayed value of 25% can mean the same thing. A date shown as a serial number may need a number format; a date that represents a different day needs a deeper check. Do not repair a display difference by overwriting a formula with its current result.

If the exported workbook triggers an Excel repair message, retain the original file, the exported file and the exact message. Try reproducing the issue in a copy with unrelated sheets removed, but do not remove material from your only original. A small, reproducible file is more useful for troubleshooting than a vague description that a large workbook looks wrong.
Build a predictable file-exchange routine

Agree on a handoff format before editing. For a normal multi-sheet workbook, use XLSX so that formulas and workbook structure have a chance to survive. Use CSV only when the recipient needs a plain data table and understands that formulas, styles and additional sheets are not the deliverable. Changing the file extension in a filename is not a conversion method; use the application’s save or export option.

Use a simple version naming rule such as inventory-source.xlsx, inventory-edited-01.xlsx and inventory-checked-01.xlsx. Keep the checked version separate from the working copy. When you send the file to someone else, describe what changed and which checks passed. This is particularly helpful if several people use different spreadsheet applications and a downloaded copy can otherwise be mistaken for the current shared version.

Common Excel compatibility questions
Does GridCraft run Excel VBA macros?
No. Keeping a VBA project in a macro-enabled file does not make its buttons, events or automation run in GridCraft. Use a supported Excel desktop workflow when execution of existing VBA is required.
Is XLSX support the same as complete Excel compatibility?

No. File support describes what an app can read and write. Compatibility also includes calculation behavior, formatting, advanced objects and how another application reads the saved result. Check the actual workbook, not just its extension.
Can I replace the original after one successful test?

Keep the original until you have checked the specific features used in the real task. A simple SUM test confirms only that example. It does not validate every chart, macro-enabled package, external reference or advanced formula in a different workbook. Keep a backup as part of the normal editing routine.
What if I only need the values from an old workbook?

A data-only import may be enough if you deliberately want a snapshot. Before using it, check whether formula results were recalculated and saved in the source app. Label the imported file as a snapshot, because a displayed total that came from a saved result will not behave like a live formula.

When GridCraft is a useful starting point

A self-contained workbook is a good evaluation case: a household budget, a small inventory, a class tracker or a personal planning sheet. You can define the expected result, inspect every important cell and keep the saved file yourself. Try the browser sample first if you want to understand the interface before installing a desktop build.

Open-source access is another reason to evaluate it: a developer can inspect the project and its documented limitations. That is useful context, but it is not evidence that a particular calculation is correct. Verify results with a small example before moving a recurring task.

When to keep Excel in the workflow

Start with the requirements that would stop your work if they failed. Examples include a VBA button that generates a report, a recurring data refresh, a shared workbook edited by several colleagues, or a customer who needs an exact Excel layout. Treat these as acceptance criteria before considering a switch.

GridCraft’s alpha status and documented gaps make advanced workbook exchange something to test, not assume. Keeping Excel for a dependency-heavy workbook while trying GridCraft on a separate, simpler task is a practical way to learn what fits. A tool does not need to replace every spreadsheet in order to be useful.

Choose one representative workbook and keep an untouched original. Write down three things that must work, such as the total, a chart and the saved output.
Make the same small edit in separate copies in both tools. Compare the displayed result and the formula text. Record any difference rather than explaining it away as a formatting issue.

Three everyday scenarios, three different decisions

A personal expense workbook has a short list of categories, a few totals and one chart. You are the only editor and can easily check the result. This is a reasonable task for evaluating GridCraft: start from a copy, make a change and reopen the saved output. The important questions are whether the calculations remain correct and whether you find the workflow comfortable enough to repeat each week.

A sales team maintains a shared forecast and several people update it during the same meeting. Here, the file is only one part of the job. Ownership, simultaneous changes, version history and access management matter too. Before moving that task, verify the complete collaboration workflow. This site’s local GridCraft editor does not provide a replacement for that shared-document process simply because it can display the spreadsheet.

An operations workbook refreshes external data and runs a VBA report every morning. The decisive test is whether the automation still runs, not whether the cells look familiar. GridCraft does not execute existing VBA, so keep a supported Excel desktop workflow for that dependency. You can still explore GridCraft with a separate exported data snapshot, provided nobody mistakes that snapshot for the automated source.
Make a decision scorecard for one workbook

List your requirements in two groups: must-have and useful. A must-have is something whose failure prevents the task from being completed, such as running an existing macro or sending an editable file to a customer. A useful feature makes the task easier but has an acceptable alternative. This prevents an attractive interface or one missing convenience from dominating a more important requirement.

Give each requirement an observable pass condition. Instead of writing “good compatibility,” write “the saved file opens in the recipient’s Excel without a repair prompt, and these three formulas match.” Instead of “easy sharing,” write down who edits, who only reads and how everyone finds the current version. Evaluate both products against the same conditions rather than relying on a general feature count.
Requirement
Pass condition
Calculation
Known inputs produce the same checked totals before and after saving.
Presentation
The chart labels, number formats and exported layout meet the recipient’s needs.
Automation
The required refresh or script actually completes the real task.
Handoff
The next person can open, inspect and continue editing the right file.
Include the cost of changing your routine

A free application can still require time to evaluate, document and teach. Count the repetitive steps you would gain or lose: downloading files, checking exported copies, explaining a new interface and fixing mismatches. For a single personal sheet, that overhead may be small. For a team passing workbooks between several systems, it can outweigh a difference in software price.

Avoid comparing a paid Excel desktop license with GridCraft without checking which Excel capabilities you actually use. If a free web edition already covers a simple collaborative task, that is a different comparison from an offline workbook with VBA. Conversely, a preference for local files or inspectable source code can be a real requirement even when a cloud option is inexpensive.

A gradual trial is easier to reverse than an all-at-once migration. Pick one low-dependency task, keep the original format and review it after a full work cycle. If it fits, expand the trial to another task. If it does not, you have learned which requirement failed without disrupting every workbook or asking colleagues to change tools before the evidence is available.
Questions that change the decision
Is GridCraft a free Excel replacement?

It is a free, open-source spreadsheet with an Excel-style workflow. Whether it replaces Excel for you depends on your files and required features. Also compare it fairly with Excel’s free web edition, not only with paid desktop plans.
Is GridCraft faster than Excel?

This guide does not establish a speed winner. A fair benchmark needs the same workbook, hardware, operation and measurement method. Time the task you actually repeat and check that both tools produce the same result.
Does using it online mean the file is shared?
No. In this site’s GridCraft editor, opening and saving are local file actions. Sending someone the editor link does not send them your workbook or your unsaved changes.
Can I use both tools instead of choosing only one?

Yes, provided you define which file is authoritative and test the exchange format. For example, keep a dependency-heavy source workbook in Excel and use a separate GridCraft copy for exploration. Make the relationship clear so edits in a downloaded copy are not silently lost when someone returns to the original.
Should the same choice apply to every colleague?

Not necessarily. The person building a report may need capabilities that a reader does not. Decide based on editing, automation and handoff requirements for each role. A shared standard can simplify support, but it should follow the real workflow rather than a general claim that one app is best for everyone.

gc.search_guides.what_is_gridcraft.descr: Learn what GridCraft is, who builds it, what its spreadsheet tools do, and how to choose between the online editor and desktop downloads.
gc.search_guides.what_is_gridcraft.intro: GridCraft is an open-source spreadsheet application built by ArtCraft in Rust. If you searched for “grid craft” or “gridcraft spreadsheet,” this is the Excel-style app for workbooks, formulas and charts. This site, gridcraft.me, is an independent guide and provides a browser entry point to the upstream app.
gc.search_guides.what_is_gridcraft.secti: The app, the project and this website

Use the ArtCraft project page and the storytold/gridcraft GitHub repository to identify the upstream software. The project publishes its source, release files and documentation there. This website adds a launch page and practical guides; it is not Microsoft Excel and is not the official ArtCraft website.

The open-source license allows use under MIT or Apache-2.0 terms. Downloading the app and using the browser build are different ways to run the software. Keep the version number with any notes about a feature: this guide references v0.19.1, and the embedded editor identifies its own build separately.
Visit the official ArtCraft product page
GridCraft v0.19.1: official project documentation
Find your way around the spreadsheet

A cell address combines a column letter and a row number. B4 means column B, row 4. The formula bar lets you inspect the selected cell’s contents, and the tabs along the bottom select worksheets. These three landmarks are enough to start exploring a sample without learning every ribbon command.

In a budget workbook, select a total to see whether it is a typed value or a formula. Then choose a nearby input cell, change one amount and watch the result. Undo the edit if you want to restore the sample. This connects the grid you see with the calculation behind it.
GridCraft formula workspace showing a gradebook and function tools
Use the formula bar to distinguish inputs from calculated results. Screenshot: ArtCraft.

Learn the formula basics
What can you do with GridCraft?
Organize tabular data: keep one kind of value in each column and one record on each row. A clear header row makes sorting, filtering and reviewing much easier.
Calculate results: use formulas for totals, comparisons and summaries. Begin with a result you can check by hand before relying on a larger model.
Make the data readable: format numbers consistently and use a chart when it helps answer a specific question, such as which category changed the most.
Summarize records: explore the sales sample and the PivotTable guide to compare groups without manually adding every row. Check the source range and totals.

Give your first session one clear goal
Choose one sample: budget for amounts, grades for formulas, or sales for charts and summaries.
Find one input and one result that depends on it. Write down what should happen when you change the input.
Make the edit, inspect the result and save a new workbook. Reopen that saved file to confirm that the change was retained.
Only then try a copy of your own file. Keep a list of missing features or differences that matter to your actual task.
A concrete example: plan a small workshop

Imagine that you are organizing a workshop and need to track three supplies. Create columns for Item, Quantity, Unit cost and Line total. Use one row for each supply, and keep the quantity and unit cost as separate numeric inputs. This structure is more useful than typing a finished total into every row because you can change attendance or prices without rewriting the entire sheet.

Start with notebooks, markers and folders. If the quantities are 12, 3 and 12, and the unit costs are 4, 6 and 2, the line totals should be 48, 18 and 24. The combined amount is 90. Enter the formulas shown below, then increase the notebook quantity from 12 to 15. The notebook total becomes 60 and the combined amount becomes 102. Those expected results give you a simple check.

Once the numbers behave as expected, apply a consistent number format and save the workbook. Reopen the saved file and repeat the quantity change. You have now practiced the essential loop: structure inputs, calculate results, make a controlled edit and keep a reusable file. The exercise also shows why a spreadsheet is different from a static table in a document.
Enter the value or formula after each cell address. This example is intentionally small enough to verify by hand.
Choose a download without guessing

Check your operating system first, then your processor architecture. A Windows x64 package and a Linux x86_64 package are not interchangeable even if the computers use similar processors. On a Mac, the pinned universal package covers Apple silicon and Intel. If you are uncertain about your machine, read its system information rather than inferring the architecture from the computer’s age or appearance.

Use the homepage download section as a starting point, then check the official release page for the filename and version. Keep the installer version in your notes. If you later report an issue or compare a desktop behavior with this site’s online editor, knowing whether both are v0.19.1 avoids confusing an upgrade with a platform difference. Downloading a newer release does not update an already open browser session.

For an initial evaluation, you do not need to install every edition. Try one representative workbook in the environment you expect to use. If the browser sample already reveals a missing requirement, investigate that requirement before spending time configuring another device. If the sample works well, a desktop trial can help you evaluate the repeated open, edit and save routine.
Review the desktop download choices
Learn in the order your workbook needs

Begin with data entry and saving. Then learn cell references and a few formulas that solve your immediate problem. After the calculations are correct, use number formats and column widths to make the sheet easier to read. Add a chart only when you can name the question it answers. This order keeps a polished-looking sheet from hiding an incorrect calculation or an unsaved file.

Move on to filters and PivotTables when the number of records makes manual inspection awkward. Before summarizing, make sure each column contains a consistent kind of value and the header row is clear. A pivot can help answer which region contributed the most revenue, but it cannot fix a source table in which quantities, labels and notes are mixed in the same column.
Continue with practical formula exercises
Build a chart or pivot after checking the data
What should you know before relying on it?
Is GridCraft ready to replace every Excel workbook?

No. The build covered here is alpha software. Small successful examples do not establish compatibility with large models, advanced objects or automation. Use the comparison guide and check the files you actually need.
Do I need a desktop app to try GridCraft?
No. The online editor lets you launch the browser build and work with a sample. A desktop browser with a keyboard is a more practical way to explore a full spreadsheet than a narrow phone screen.
What is the difference between a workbook and a worksheet?

A workbook is the file you open and save. It can contain several worksheets, each represented by a sheet tab. When checking an imported file, inspect more than the first worksheet: other sheets may contain inputs, lookup data or formulas that the visible summary depends on.
Can I learn with GridCraft before moving my own files?

Yes. The supplied samples let you inspect a finished workbook and make reversible edits. Use the small workshop example for a second exercise, then try an independent copy of a file you understand. Keep the learning session separate from the original file you depend on for real work.

Start with a sample or open a local workbook, make a change, then save a downloaded copy before leaving. The link to the editor opens the app; it does not contain your workbook or synchronize your edits to another device.
gc.search_guides.gridcraft_online.sectio: Launch GridCraft in the browser

Open the online editor from the homepage. Choose Blank workbook or one of the three samples: Sales dashboard, Monthly budget or Grade tracker. A sample gives you meaningful data to inspect immediately; a blank workbook is better when you want to enter a small example of your own.
Choose Monthly budget for this walkthrough, then select Launch GridCraft.
Wait for the spreadsheet grid to appear. The first launch needs to load the browser app; a visible loading message is not yet an editable workbook.
Click inside the spreadsheet before using its keyboard shortcuts. The editor runs in an embedded frame, so keyboard focus matters.
Gridcraft.me launch screen with a Launch GridCraft button and four starting-point choices
The launch screen lets you choose a sample before starting. Captured on gridcraft.me’s local preview, November 2026.
Launch the budget sample online
Open your file or make one small edit

To use your own spreadsheet, choose File → Open inside GridCraft and select a copy of an .xlsx workbook. The application opens the browser file picker. Keep the source file until you have checked the downloaded result. For more complex Excel files, follow the compatibility guide before editing important data.

For a first edit, select an ordinary input cell rather than a total. Note its value, change it by a small amount and press Enter. Select a related formula cell to inspect the result. If you accidentally replace a formula, use Undo and return to the input cell.
Check XLSX compatibility before importing
Follow the first-workbook exercise
Save a file you can actually reopen
Commit any active cell edit with Enter. Then choose File → Save As in the editor.
Use an .xlsx filename for a normal workbook, for example budget-online-test.xlsx. The browser build saves by downloading a file rather than updating a cloud document.
Check that the download completed. Find the newest file in your browser’s download list; repeated downloads can have similar names.
Reopen the saved copy through File → Open and check the edited cell and a dependent total. Only close the session after you have a file with the changes you expect.

Do not use a refresh or a reopened editor URL as a saving test. A fresh session can start from the original sample. The downloaded workbook is the portable copy you can move to a desktop app, another browser or another person.
GridCraft sales chart with formatting tools and its source table visible
After reopening, check objects such as charts as well as cell values. Screenshot: ArtCraft.
If the online editor does not start

What to try

Check the connection and try again. If the error panel offers Open with WebGL, use that fallback.

Click a cell inside the editor first. For more room, use the full-screen or open-in-a-tab control.
No file appears after saving
Inspect the browser’s download list and any blocked-download notice. Keep the workbook open while checking.
The workbook is too awkward on a phone
Use a desktop browser and keyboard, or choose a desktop build for regular work.

The browser build needs supported graphics capabilities: WebGPU or WebGL2. A device or browser without either cannot display the editor. If one workbook fails but a sample works, investigate that file separately instead of repeatedly reloading the page with unsaved work.
Find a desktop version on the homepage
A focused first ten minutes online

Use the first few minutes to find the input cells, formula bar and sheet tabs in the budget sample. Select a category amount and read the formula bar before changing it. This tells you whether you are looking at a typed input or a calculated result. If a total is based on other cells, edit those inputs instead of replacing the total with a number that only looks correct.

Next, make one change you can predict. For example, increase a single expense by 5 and check whether the relevant total increases by 5. If the workbook includes a budget-versus-actual comparison, identify which number represents the plan and which represents the expense. Changing the planned amount is a different action from changing the actual amount, even when the two columns use the same currency format.

Finish the session by saving a clearly named test file and reopening it. Keep your test deliberately small: one input, one calculated result and one saved copy. This establishes the whole online workflow before you spend time formatting a large table or importing a workbook whose dependencies you have not inspected. You should be able to point to the file that now contains your change.
Keep browser downloads easy to identify

Create a dedicated folder for the files you use in this exercise. Keep the original workbook there under a source name, and put each downloaded result under a name that describes its purpose. A filename such as workshop-review-02.xlsx is easier to recognize than several copies called Book1.xlsx. The exact naming pattern matters less than consistently distinguishing the untouched original from the file you just edited.

When a browser adds a number to a repeated download, do not assume the unnumbered file is the latest. Check the download time and reopen the file you actually intend to keep. If the file is going to another person, test that exact copy rather than a different version still open in the editor. A successful calculation in memory does not verify the contents of an older file sitting in a downloads folder.

For a longer session, save at meaningful checkpoints: after importing and checking a file, after making the main edits, and before closing or switching devices. This is a manual file workflow. Treat an open tab as a workspace, not a backup. If you need a continuously shared document with other editors, first choose a workflow designed for that requirement instead of forwarding this editor URL.
Separate a loading problem from a file problem

If the application fails before a sample grid appears, begin with the browser environment. Confirm that the connection can load the application, check the displayed error, and use the offered WebGL fallback if appropriate. Retrying with a small sample is more informative than repeatedly opening a complex workbook while the graphics runtime itself is not starting. The fallback is a renderer choice, not a repair tool for workbook data.

If a sample works but your own file does not, preserve the original and inspect the file type and size. Try a smaller copy with only the relevant sheet, or a simple XLSX workbook whose result you know. Do not diagnose every file failure as a browser problem. The compatibility guide explains why a supported extension still does not guarantee that every advanced object or calculation will behave as expected.

If the file opens but interaction feels slow, keep the test controlled. Compare a small sample with the same workbook, close unrelated heavy tabs, and note the action that stalls: launch, import, recalculation or scrolling. Those are different operations. Record the browser, device and GridCraft version when investigating so that a future test compares the same conditions rather than a different setup.
Troubleshoot a workbook mismatch
Questions about online use
Do I have to install GridCraft first?
No desktop installation is needed for the browser editor. The browser still needs to load the application files before the workspace starts.
Will my workbook appear on another device?
Not from the editor URL alone. Save and transfer the workbook file, then open that file on the other device. Signing into this website is not a substitute for saving a workbook.
Is the browser editor the newest GridCraft release?

The editor displays its bundled version on its start screen. The current desktop download links point to official v0.19.1 packages. Desktop downloads and the bundled browser editor are updated separately, so check both labels before comparing their behavior.
Can I return later using the same editor link?

You can use the link to open the application again, but keep your saved workbook separately. To continue from your own changes, open the downloaded file in the new session. A sample parameter in the URL chooses a starting sample; it is not a reference to your edited copy.
Why does a keyboard shortcut do nothing?

First click inside the spreadsheet and make sure a dialog or text-editing control is not using the keyboard. Some shortcuts can also be reserved by the browser or operating system. Use the visible menu command when the shortcut is unavailable, and avoid testing destructive commands on your only copy.

gc.tested_guides.vlookup_xlookup.intro: A lookup that returns a number can still return the wrong record. We tested VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP with the official GridCraft v0.19.1 CLI on macOS on November 13, 2026. These are calculation-engine checks, not a claim that every Excel lookup workbook or browser version behaves identically. The small duplicate-key example below makes the differences visible before you use either function in a real report.
gc.tested_guides.vlookup_xlookup.section: Start with a lookup table you can check by eye

Put Code and Price in A1:B1. Enter four rows: 10 and 100; 20 and 200; 20 and 250; 30 and 300. The repeated code 20 is deliberate. It lets us distinguish the first matching row from the last, while the missing code 25 tests approximate matching. Keep the lookup column numeric throughout this first check.

Download the CSV example and open it in the tested release, or enter the values manually. For a repeatable command-line check, run the expression with gridcraft-cli eval, passing --in lookup.csv and --json. In a worksheet, enter it in an unused cell outside A1:B5. Do not accidentally replace a lookup value with the formula you are testing.
Both expressions returned 200 in our v0.19.1 check.
Download the four-row lookup example
VLOOKUP: exact, approximate, and invalid column numbers

The supported signature has three required arguments and an optional fourth: VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]). With FALSE, the code 20 returned 200, the first matching row. Code 25 returned #N/A because no exact record exists. This is a useful failure: it exposes a missing key instead of silently choosing a nearby price.

With TRUE and the ascending example, code 25 returned 250, the price from the last qualifying row with code 20. Approximate matching therefore did not mean “find the closest number in either direction.” Use a deliberately sorted table for this check and do not assume an unsorted price list is safe. Explicitly choose FALSE for identifiers, invoice numbers, and product codes when exact identity matters.

XLOOKUP: fallback values and search direction

XLOOKUP accepts lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, then optional if_not_found, match_mode, and search_mode. In our example, the three-argument form returned 200. Searching for 99 with a fallback of "missing" returned that text. This is clearer than wrapping every lookup in broad error suppression, because unrelated structural errors should still be investigated.

The optional match mode changed the result for code 25: -1 returned 200 and 1 returned 300. With an exact code 20 and search mode -1, the result became 250, the last duplicate. Search mode 2 returned 200 on the ascending sample. These checks establish those particular cases; descending binary searches, wildcard patterns, and spilled multi-column results were not covered by this test set.

An unsupported match mode of 7 and an unsupported search mode of 7 both returned #VALUE!. Using A2:A5 as the lookup range but B2:B4 as the return range also returned #VALUE!. A fallback string did not turn an invalid mode into a successful lookup. Keep both arrays aligned and the same size before investigating missing keys.
Observed results, in order: missing, 200, 250.
Move from the sample to your workbook

First decide whether duplicate keys are valid in your data. If they are, document whether the first or last record should win. Next check whether imported codes are numbers or text: a successful numeric example does not prove that "0012" and 12 are interchangeable identifiers. Check missing keys separately from malformed ranges, and verify a few returned records against their source rows.

Save a copy as XLSX and reopen it in the application where the file will be used. Recheck the missing key and duplicate key, not just one successful result. If an expression is rejected before calculation, inspect the required arguments and separators; if it calculates to an error value, investigate that specific error. The v0.19.1 CLI exits unsuccessfully for the too-few-arguments examples, whereas calculated spreadsheet errors are returned as values in JSON.

gc.tested_guides.pivot_table_tutorial.in: A useful first PivotTable is small enough to verify without trusting the software. We created the following report with GridCraft v0.19.1 commands, saved it as XLSX, and opened the exported workbook in the v0.19.1 browser build in Tabbit on macOS. The summary cells and the North/South column chart were visible after reopening. The example is intentionally modest: it tests the path from source rows to a saved report, not every pivot feature.
gc.tested_guides.pivot_table_tutorial.se: Prepare a rectangular source table

Use one header row with Region, Product, and Revenue in A1:C1. Add North / Studio / 480, South / Studio / 320, and North / Workshop / 240. Keep Revenue numeric. Do not add a precomputed grand-total row to the source: a pivot could count that row along with the original records and double the revenue.

For a first attempt, avoid merged headings, blank header cells, and decorative notes inside the data rectangle. Those choices make it harder to tell which field is being summarized. Before inserting anything, calculate the expected answer: North is 480 + 240 = 720, South is 320, and the complete dataset sums to 1,040. Write those checks beside your working notes.
Three records, two regions, and one numeric measure.
Create the report and choose Sum

Select the source rectangle and use Insert > PivotTable. Choose a new sheet for the destination so the summary cannot overwrite the original rows. Put Region in Rows and Revenue in Values. Check that the value field uses Sum, because a count of records answers a different question. The field list is the place to inspect which fields are assigned to each area.

Our reproducible command used source Sheet1!A1:C4, rows ["Region"], and a Revenue value field with func "sum". GridCraft created a new sheet, placed the report at A3:B6, and named the value column Sum of Revenue. The results matched the hand calculation. Keeping this exact source range in the test makes it clear which records were included.

Turn the summary into a column chart

Select a cell in the report and choose Insert > PivotChart. Use a column chart with a descriptive title such as Revenue by region. This gives you a compact comparison of the two regions. Keep the unit clear; a number without a currency or other business context may be mathematically correct but confusing to the reader.

In the tested command workflow, insert.pivotChart referenced the named RevenueByRegion pivot and returned one chart with one series. After saving and reopening the XLSX file in the browser build, the chart showed North and South alongside the report. The grand total stayed in the summary table rather than becoming a third region in the pictured chart. That visual check matters: the report can be correct while the chosen chart categories are misleading.

Check the source and refresh deliberately

When you change the original data, refresh the PivotTable and compare the new total with the source again. A fixed range such as A1:C4 does not describe a new record on row 5. Check Change Data Source or use a correctly defined table before assuming the next refresh includes appended rows. The v0.19.1 command catalog provides pivot.refresh and pivot.changeSource; the saved-file check above did not exercise every combination of source expansion and filters.

If the summary looks wrong, inspect the source range first, then the aggregation function and active filters. A text-looking number can also change which summaries are meaningful. Keep a small unfiltered report as a reference while experimenting with Product in Columns or additional value fields. Save a working copy before changing a report that somebody else relies on.

Finally, reopen the exported workbook and verify the labels, values, and chart. If the destination is Excel, perform that final check in Excel too; our test verified reopening in GridCraft only. A successful GridCraft round trip is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for testing the actual recipient’s application.

gc.tested_guides.csv_import_export.intro: CSV looks simple because it is plain text, but it leaves important interpretation decisions to the application opening it. We checked small CSV and TSV fixtures using the official GridCraft v0.19.1 CLI on macOS. The results below separate the bytes in the source from the values GridCraft displayed. This distinction explains why a file can open successfully and still change an identifier or a date.
gc.tested_guides.csv_import_export.secti: Start with readable characters and correctly quoted fields

Our UTF-8 fixture contained a byte-order mark, Café, and 上海. Both names survived the import check. A separate Windows-1252 fixture containing Café also opened correctly. That is evidence for these fixtures, not a promise that every legacy encoding will be recognized. If names become replacement characters or mojibake, return to the source file and export a fresh UTF-8 copy before editing the corrupted values.

We also checked a quoted field containing North, Inc. and a note containing an embedded double quote. The quoted comma stayed inside one field, and the quote was escaped correctly in the CSV output. When preparing a file by hand, quote fields that contain delimiters or line breaks, and double an embedded quotation mark. Changing the delimiter alone cannot repair malformed quoting.
Download the UTF-8 names, dates, and codes fixture
Download the quoted-comma example
Comma, semicolon, and tab examples

A two-column semicolon-separated .csv file opened as two fields in our check. A .tsv file separated by tabs also opened as two fields. The sample values 12.50 and 8 became numeric values. These cases are useful for exports from different regional settings, but the test did not cover decimal commas mixed with semicolon separators or every text-export dialect.

Inspect the first few records immediately after opening. If an entire row appears in one cell, the import has not produced the table you expected. If a company name has become two columns, inspect quoting around its comma. Confirm the header count and the record count before writing formulas against the imported range; a plausible-looking total can hide a shifted column.

Leading zeros and dates need an explicit decision

The default import converted code 0012 to numeric 12 and code 0007 to 7. That is reasonable for quantities and wrong for identifiers whose width is meaningful. The amount 12.50 displayed as 12.5. A different display does not necessarily mean a different numeric value, but missing zeros in a customer code can change its meaning completely.

The ISO date 2026-11-12 remained recognizable as a date in the displayed output. The ambiguous 03/04/2026 produced a warning saying it was read month first. Do not infer the intended date from its appearance alone: March 4 and April 3 are both valid dates. Prefer an unambiguous source format, and check known examples before accepting a whole column.

The file.open command supports csvAsText: true. In that test, 0012, 0007, 12.50, and both date strings stayed exactly as text. That mode is a useful preservation option for automation, although it also means arithmetic and date operations need deliberate conversion later. It is not evidence that every graphical import screen exposes the same switch.
A v0.19.1 CLI run script can preserve every imported field as text.
Check the exported file, not only the open sheet

CSV is a single-sheet text exchange format. It is not a replacement for an XLSX master containing multiple sheets, charts, styles, or pivot definitions. Save a workbook copy first, then export the intended sheet and reopen the resulting text file. Verify the same names, identifiers, date examples, and totals in the receiving tool.

The v0.19.1 command catalog distinguishes displayed-value CSV export from raw-value export with values: true. Pick the representation the next tool expects, then verify it rather than assuming formatting is portable. A numeric amount and its currency-formatted display serve different purposes. Our fixture checks used CLI CSV output; they do not establish every formatted export option.

One additional trap appeared while preparing the large-sheet test: a CSV field beginning with =C2*D2 imported as text, rather than becoming a working formula. We explicitly entered a formula and filled it down in GridCraft before testing recalculation. If imported formulas appear inert, check whether the cells contain text before changing calculation settings.

Formula troubleshooting
7 min read
GridCraft Formulas Not Recalculating: A Practical Checklist — spreadsheet example
Upstream GridCraft example, used to illustrate the workflow. This image is not evidence of the test results below.

A stale result is not always a broken calculation engine. It can come from manual calculation mode, a formula stored as text, or a reference that never pointed at the edited cell. We reproduced these cases with the official GridCraft v0.19.1 CLI on macOS. Start with a copy of your workbook and a tiny example; the goal is to identify the cause before changing settings across the entire file.
Establish whether a simple dependency works

In a new workbook, put 2 in A1 and =A1*3 in B1. Our result was 6. Changing A1 to 5 changed B1 to 15 in automatic mode. This gives you a baseline independent of imported styles, named ranges, external links, and a complicated existing formula. If the simple case works, narrow the investigation to the original workbook rather than assuming every calculation is failing.

Check the formula bar as well as the displayed result. A copied formula may point at a different row, and an absolute reference such as $A$1 deliberately stays fixed. Compare the exact reference with the cell you edited. A mathematically correct formula that references the wrong cell will keep returning a perfectly plausible value.
The automatic-calculation baseline passed in v0.19.1.
Inspect Calculation Options before forcing a refresh

We then set Calculation Options to manual. Changing A1 from 5 to 7 left B1 at 15. Executing Calculate Now changed B1 to 21. That reproduces an apparently stuck formula without any broken reference. In the interface, look under Formulas > Calculation; the command catalog identifies Calculate Now as F9 and Calculate Sheet as Shift+F9. On keyboards where function keys control hardware, the ribbon action may be simpler.

If a workbook was intentionally set to manual because it is expensive to recalculate, understand that choice before switching modes. For everyday files, automatic calculation avoids the surprise of looking at yesterday’s cached result. A forced recalculation is a diagnostic step, not proof that every imported formula is supported or that every external data source refreshed.

A formula-shaped string may be ordinary text

We entered an apostrophe followed by =A1*3. GridCraft stored a string displaying =A1*3 rather than a calculated result. Pressing Calculate Now cannot turn that text into a dependency. The same distinction appeared when a formula-shaped CSV field was imported during our large-sheet preparation. Inspect the cell type and the actual input before assuming calculation mode is responsible.

On a disposable copy, re-enter one formula without a leading apostrophe and confirm the expected result. Do not blindly remove apostrophes from a whole imported sheet: some cells are intentionally text, including product codes, examples, and strings supplied by other people. A small successful correction tells you what to fix while preserving the original data for comparison.
Separate circular references from cross-sheet dependencies

With iterative calculation disabled, =C1+1 in C1 returned #CIRC! in our test. The formula needs its own answer to produce its answer. Trace the dependency chain and remove the unintended loop. Iterative calculation is a separate modeling choice; turning it on to silence a warning can hide a mistake instead of resolving it.

Cross-sheet calculation worked in the simple case. Sheet1!A1 contained 10, and Sheet2!A1 contained =Sheet1!A1*2, producing 20. After changing the source to 12, the dependent cell became 24. This establishes an ordinary internal sheet reference, not an external workbook link. Check sheet names, renamed ranges, and missing source cells when your own cross-sheet example fails.

A sheet name containing spaces needs the appropriate quoted reference syntax, for example ='Sales Data'!A1*2. Inspect the expression after moving or copying it. If a workbook was imported from another application, reduce the formula to one source cell, then restore the additional operations one by one until the difference appears.
Keep a minimal reproduction for unresolved cases

Record the application version, calculation mode, exact formula, source values, and observed result. Replace confidential values with a small invented example that still fails. Compare a new workbook with the imported workbook, then save and reopen a copy to see whether the problem is tied to loading or to editing.

If the reduced example still fails, consult the supported function signature and the upstream issue tracker. Include whether the formula was rejected on entry or accepted and evaluated to an error. Those are different failure stages and need different evidence. Our checks cover the cases shown here; they do not validate macros, external data refresh, or every volatile function.

Qualitative observations from a v0.19.1 browser workbook with 12,000 records and a simple formula column, plus a repeatable way to test your own files.
Performance test
7 min read
GridCraft with 12,000 Rows: Practical Performance Notes — spreadsheet example
Our v0.19.1 test workbook, opened in Tabbit on macOS. See the test scope below.

A row count is useful context, but it does not describe the whole workload. We opened a synthetic 12,000-record workbook in the official GridCraft v0.19.1 browser build, served locally and operated in Tabbit on macOS on November 13, 2026. This is a qualitative spot check of one environment. We report responsive operations and noticeable waiting rather than presenting a universal speed score or a promise about your device.
What was in the test workbook

The sheet had five columns: ID, Region, Units, Price, and Revenue. It contained 12,000 data rows plus the header, so its used range was A1:E12001 and it held 60,005 cells. Regions repeated North, South, East, and West; units varied; the price was 12.5. Revenue used a simple same-row multiplication. There were no images, pivot tables, charts, merged cells, conditional-format rules, or external links in this test.

We first prepared the values as CSV and converted them to XLSX with the v0.19.1 CLI. The formula-looking CSV fields were text on import, so we explicitly entered =C2*D2 in E2 and used Fill Down through E12001. That correction matters: scrolling a sheet of text would not test a workbook with 12,000 active arithmetic formulas. We checked the final formula results before drawing any conclusions.
What felt responsive, and what involved waiting

Opening the workbook completed and the grid remained usable. Wheel scrolling and Page Down moved the viewport without an obvious sustained stall in our spot checks. Selecting a distant cell and editing one input also completed without a disruptive wait. These observations describe the interactions we checked; screenshots alone cannot establish perfectly smooth animation throughout a long session.

Bulk filling the entire formula column was noticeably heavier than editing one cell. There was a clear wait before the command finished and the updated values could be checked. After the fill completed, normal navigation remained responsive. Treat a large batch operation as a different workload from moving around an already calculated sheet.

At the end of the sheet, changing Units to 20 produced Revenue 250 with Price 12.5. Sorting all five columns by ID descending also completed without a disruptive stall in this sample. We checked that the first records were 12000, 11999, and 11998 and that their units, prices, and revenues stayed together. A visually sorted ID column alone would not establish that the complete rows were sorted correctly.

What this result does not establish

This workbook was narrow and deliberately simple. Thousands of lookup formulas over wide ranges, many chart objects, elaborate conditional formatting, or a deep chain of dependent sheets can create a very different workload at the same row count. We did not run a long-duration stability test, a mobile test, or a comparison against Excel on identical hardware.

The browser build was a separate local v0.19.1 test installation. Check the version shown by this website’s embedded editor before treating it as the same build. Browser graphics support, available memory, other open tabs, and desktop versus web packaging can affect the experience. Do not turn one successful sample into a general recommendation to move a critical workbook without checking its actual operations.
Repeat the checks with a copy of your own workbook

Start by writing down the used range, formula count or approximate density, and the features that matter to your workflow. Open a copy, navigate between distant rows, edit a source value, sort a complete table, and run the most common report operation. Check correctness after each action. Keep the same application version and similar background workload when comparing two versions.

Use descriptions that another person can understand: navigation remained responsive; a bulk fill caused a noticeable wait; a calculation left the interface unresponsive; reopening lost a feature. Separate initial loading, ordinary navigation, bulk edits, and recalculation. Averaging those experiences into one claim hides the part that may matter most to your work.

If a workbook struggles, reduce one source of complexity at a time on a copy. Compare a values-only sheet with the formula version, then add formatting and objects back. Keep referenced ranges as focused as the calculation allows, and save before expensive structural edits. A small reproducible workbook is more useful for an upstream report than a vague statement that “large files are slow.”
